knowledge_point.title: Determining an Amount at an Overflow Point

question.:question/problem: A coolant reservoir in a manufacturing plant can hold up to $240\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $90\,\text{gal}$ of coolant solution with $18\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved corrosion inhibitor. A more concentrated coolant solution with concentration $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which inhibitor enters the reservoir minus the rate at which inhibitor leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which inhibitor enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of inhibitor enters the reservoir at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *inhibitor* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =9\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which inhibitor exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which inhibitor leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $90\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $18\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $12\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=90+18t-12t=6(15+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *inhibitor* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{15+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{15+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q=9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(15+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|15+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(15+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(15+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q) & =(15+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (15+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(15+t)Q & =9(15+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2}) & =9(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(15+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(15+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(15+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(15+t)+\frac{C}{(15+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of inhibitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ 3(15+0)+\frac{C}{(15+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ 45+\frac{C}{(15)^{2}} & =18 \\ \frac{C}{{15}^{2}} & =-27 \\ C & =-27(15)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(15+t)-\frac{27(15)^{2}}{(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(15+t)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $240\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=240$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =240 \\ 90+18{t}_{o}-12{t}_{o} & =240 \\ 90+6{t}_{o} & =240 \\ 6{t}_{o} & =150 \\ {t}_{o} & =25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of inhibitor in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(25) & =3(15+25)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+25}\right)}^{2} \\  & =120-27{\left(\frac{15}{40}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈116.2\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: 0 <= t <= overflow onset; capacity > initial volume, inflow > outflow, incoming concentration > initial concentration

question.:question/problem: A wastewater treatment tank at a chemical plant can hold up to $372\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $210\,\text{gal}$ of wastewater with $56\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved contaminant. A more concentrated wastewater stream with concentration $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminant enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =14.4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $210\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $18\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $12\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=210+18t-12t=6(35+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{6(35+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(35+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(35+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{6(35+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{35+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =14.4-\frac{2Q}{35+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{35+t}\,Q=14.4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(35+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|35+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(35+t)^{2}} \\  & =(35+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(35+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(35+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{35+t}\,Q) & =(35+t)^{2}\cdot 14.4 \\ (35+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(35+t)Q & =14.4(35+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(35+t)^{2}) & =14.4(35+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(35+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 14.4(35+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(35+t)^{2} & =14.4\cdot \frac{1}{3}(35+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =4.8(35+t)+\frac{C}{(35+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $56\,\text{lb}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=56,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =56 \\ 4.8(35+0)+\frac{C}{(35+0)^{2}} & =56 \\ 168+\frac{C}{(35)^{2}} & =56 \\ \frac{C}{{35}^{2}} & =-112 \\ C & =-112(35)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =4.8(35+t)-\frac{112(35)^{2}}{(35+t)^{2}} \\  & =4.8(35+t)-112{\left(\frac{35}{35+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $372\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=372$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =372 \\ 210+18{t}_{o}-12{t}_{o} & =372 \\ 210+6{t}_{o} & =372 \\ 6{t}_{o} & =162 \\ {t}_{o} & =27\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(27) & =4.8(35+27)-112{\left(\frac{35}{35+27}\right)}^{2} \\  & =297.6-112{\left(\frac{35}{62}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈261.9\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: 0 <= t <= overflow onset; capacity > initial volume, inflow > outflow, incoming concentration > initial concentration
